Investigating the Impact of Political Marketing on Electoral Patronage Behaviour

Abstract:

Electoral democracies have increasingly witnessed the systematic application of marketing techniques in political communication, as traditional ideological and policy-based appeals are complemented by leadership positioning and digitally mediated campaign strategies. This transformation has intensified electoral competition and reshaped voter&ndashparty relationships, particularly among younger cohorts who are highly exposed to symbolic and personalised political communication. Despite the growing prominence of political marketing, existing research has largely focused on short-term outcomes such as voting intention, candidate evaluation, and campaign persuasion, while comparatively limited attention has been given to long-term electoral patronage behaviour. Moreover, empirical studies examining how multiple political marketing dimensions collectively influence sustained voter loyalty remain fragmented, particularly within emerging democratic contexts. Addressing this gap, the present study investigates the influence of key political marketing dimensions, namely political brand personality, political brand trust, political brand image, and welfare policy perception, on electoral patronage behaviour among Gen Z voters in selected states of Eastern India, specifically West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Bihar. The study conceptualises political brand preference as a central mechanism through which these dimensions shape long-term voter loyalty and repeated electoral support, while self-political brand connection captures identity-based variations in this relationship. The study is grounded in an integrated theoretical framework comprising the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Social Identity Theory, and the ABC Model of Attitude. The ABC model explains the cognitive and affective formation of political brand preference, the Theory of Planned Behaviour establishes the attitudinal&ndashbehavioural linkage, and Social Identity Theory explains the role of identity alignment in shaping electoral behaviour. Methodologically, the study adopts an explanatory sequential mixed-method approach, integrating qualitative exploration with quantitative survey data analysed utilising Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). By shifting the analytical focus from short-term voting intention to sustained electoral patronage behaviour, the study strengthens the literature by offering a multidimensional and theory-driven explanation of voter loyalty within a complex multi-party democratic context.
